timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: IP addresses are just like home addresses for computers, right?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Correct. And subnetting is like zip codes — it groups devices into neighborhoods.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Why does that matter for security?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Because if you put all your devices in one subnet, an attacker who compromises one can reach all of them.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So smaller subnets are more secure?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Yes. Network segmentation limits lateral movement. A /28 subnet holds only 14 hosts — much harder to pivot through.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: You forge the source address to impersonate another machine. Amplification attacks use this to redirect responses to a victim.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Can't firewalls just block spoofed IPs?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: They can with ingress filtering — checking that source IPs are valid for the network they come from. But many don't.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Attackers split packets into tiny fragments to bypass IDS rules that only inspect the first fragment.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So understanding IP is really about understanding how to build secure network boundaries?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Exactly. Without IP knowledge, you're building walls without knowing where the doors are.
